evidence.quote: The free-threaded build of Python is now supported and no longer experimental. This is the start of phase II where free-threaded Python is officially supported but still optional.

evidence.quote: Any decision to transition to phase III, with free-threading as the default or sole build of Python is still undecided, and dependent on many factors both within CPython itself and the community.

claims.text: Whether to move to phase III, with free-threading as the default or only build, is still undecided.

evidence.quote: The performance penalty on single-threaded code in free-threaded mode is now roughly 5-10%, depending on the platform and C compiler used.

evidence.quote: Phase II would make the free-threaded build officially supported but still optional, and phase III would make the free-threaded build the default.

claims.text: PEP 779 defines three phases: phase I experimental, phase II officially supported but optional, phase III free-threaded build as the default.

evidence.quote: Free-threaded execution allows for full utilization of the available processing power by running threads in parallel on available CPU cores.

evidence.quote: While not all software will benefit from this automatically, programs designed with threading in mind will run faster on multi-core hardware.

evidence.quote: Some third-party packages, in particular ones with an extension module, may not be ready for use in a free-threaded build, and will re-enable the GIL.

evidence.quote: Starting with Python 3.13, the official macOS and Windows installers optionally support installing free-threaded Python binaries.

evidence.quote: When building CPython from source, the --disable-gil configure option should be used to build a free-threaded Python interpreter.

evidence.quote: To check if the current interpreter supports free-threading, python -VV and sys.version contain “free-threading build”.

evidence.quote: The new sys._is_gil_enabled() function can be used to check whether the GIL is actually disabled in the running process.

evidence.quote: The sysconfig.get_config_var("Py_GIL_DISABLED") configuration variable can be used to determine whether the build supports free threading. If the variable is set to 1, then the build supports free threading. This is the recommended mechanism for decisions related to the build configuration.

evidence.quote: Free-threaded builds of CPython support optionally running with the GIL enabled at runtime using the environment variable PYTHON_GIL or the command-line option -X gil.

claims.text: Free-threaded builds can optionally run with the GIL enabled at runtime, controlled by the PYTHON_GIL environment variable or the -X gil option.

evidence.quote: The GIL may also automatically be enabled when importing a C-API extension module that is not explicitly marked as supporting free threading. A warning will be printed in this case.

evidence.quote: It’s recommended to use the threading.Lock or other synchronization primitives instead of relying on the internal locks of built-in types, when possible.

evidence.quote: On the pyperformance benchmark suite, the average overhead ranges from about 1% on macOS aarch64 to 8% on x86-64 Linux systems.

claims.text: The free-threading HOWTO puts the average pyperformance overhead at about 1% on macOS aarch64 to 8% on x86-64 Linux, depending on workload and hardware.

evidence.quote: The free-threaded build will typically use more memory compared to the default build.

claims.text: The free-threaded build typically uses more memory than the default build.

evidence.quote: -X gil=0,1 forces the GIL to be disabled or enabled, respectively. Setting to 0 is only available in builds configured with --disable-gil.

evidence.quote: If this variable is set to 1, the global interpreter lock (GIL) will be forced on. Setting it to 0 forces the GIL off (needs Python configured with the --disable-gil build option). See also the -X gil command-line option, which takes precedence over this variable

content.applies_to: CPython 3.14 documentation (What's New in 3.14, free-threading HOWTOs, command line page) and PEP 779 (status Final), read on 2026-11-11. Not other Python implementations.
not_covered: The cited pages give different single-threaded overhead figures (What's New: roughly 5-10%; free-threading HOWTO: about 1% to 8% average); both are quoted, neither was measured here.
PEP 779's performance and memory numbers describe the state when the PEP was written, before 3.14's final release.
No local benchmark was run; nothing here covers PyPy, GraalPy or other Python implementations.
Which specific third-party packages support free threading was not checked.
recommendations: Recommendation / inference: do not assume upgrading to 3.14 removes the GIL: install or build the free-threaded interpreter explicitly (installer option or --disable-gil).

Recommendation / inference: check both the build (sysconfig.get_config_var("Py_GIL_DISABLED") == 1 or 'free-threading build' in sys.version) and the running process (sys._is_gil_enabled()) after all imports.
Recommendation / inference: use PYTHON_GIL=0 or -X gil=0 only on a free-threaded build to force the GIL off while testing; remember that -X gil overrides PYTHON_GIL.
Recommendation / inference: check that every C extension you import declares free-threading support and ships t-suffixed wheels; watch for the GIL re-enable warning.
Recommendation / inference: measure the same representative workload with one and several threads and verify output correctness; expect single-threaded slowdown and higher memory use.
Recommendation / inference: protect shared application state with threading.Lock or other explicit synchronization instead of relying on built-in types' internal locks.
content.short_answer: In 3.14 the free-threaded build is officially supported but still optional (PEP 779, phase II); the default build keeps the GIL. A free-threaded build shows 'free-threading build' in python -VV and sys.version, and sysconfig.get_config_var("Py_GIL_DISABLED") is 1; sys._is_gil_enabled() tells whether the GIL is actually off. PYTHON_GIL=0/1 or -X gil=0/1 force it off/on (0 needs a --disable-gil build). Unmarked C extensions re-enable the GIL with a warning. Speedups are not automatic, and single-threaded code is slower.
